Beulah
BYOO-lah
proper n. (Hebrew prophetic name of the land of Israel)
Hebrew be'ulah, passive participle of ba'al, to marry, to be lord over: married, possessed as a wife.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Beulah occurs once, as the land's new name. “Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzibah, and thy land Beulah: for the LORD delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married” (Isaiah 62:4). The desolate land is pictured as a widow or an abandoned wife, and God declares her married. Isaiah had already given the ground of it: “For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name” (Isaiah 54:5). The marriage image runs from the prophets to the last pages of the Bible, where John sees the holy city “prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). Beulah is therefore not first a pleasant country but a covenant status: the land and people the LORD has taken to Himself, never again to be called Desolate.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Beulah; the word is a Hebrew prophetic name carried into the Authorized Version untranslated.

Webster (1828) gives no entry for Beulah.

The name is the Hebrew be'ulah, married.

It occurs once, at Isaiah 62:4, as the new name of the land.

It stands opposite the old name Desolate.

Bunyan borrowed it for the Country of Beulah in The Pilgrim's Progress.

Key Scripture

Isa 62:4 — "Thou shalt no more be termed Forsaken; neither shall thy land any more be termed Desolate: but thou shalt be called Hephzibah, and thy land Beulah: for the LORD delighteth in thee, and thy land shall be married."

Isa 54:5 — "For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called."

Rev 21:2 — "And I John saw the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband."

Modern Corruption

Beulah became, in revival hymnody, a sentimental land of rest on the near side of death, its covenant meaning traded for a mood.

expand to see more

The nineteenth-century gospel song Beulah Land, drawing on Bunyan's Country of Beulah in The Pilgrim's Progress, made the word a byword for the sweet borderland of heaven. Bunyan used it as allegory and knew what he was doing; later popular use often kept the sweetness and lost the marriage.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Beulah means married. The comfort of the name rests entirely on the Husband: the LORD who made the land, redeemed the people, and will present the church to Himself as a bride without spot.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew be'ulah, married, from ba'al, to marry; the land renamed as a wife.

expand to see more

Hebrew ba'al, to marry, to rule over as husband.

Hebrew be'ulah, a married woman, a wife.

Isaiah 62:4 gives Beulah as the land's new name.

Isaiah 54:5 names the LORD of hosts as the husband of His people.

Revelation 21:2 completes the image in the bride, the new Jerusalem.

"the land declared married"

"the Husband who makes the desolate a wife"
